lead: A starter cranks a cold engine in under two seconds. It needs maximum torque at zero speed, a drive that grips the flywheel only while cranking, and a switch that carries hundreds of amperes without burning the key. A small control current works a relay and solenoid; the solenoid meshes the pinion and closes the heavy contacts. The chapter covers motor types, drives, and control and power circuits. The torque and speed the engine demands come from Chapter 1.9.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.9 for cranking torque and minimum starting speed, and Chapter 1.5 for cold cranking amps.

blocks.text: A starter is a DC motor built for one duty: maximum torque at zero speed, for a few seconds, a few times an hour.

In a series-wound motor the field winding is in series with the armature. At standstill back emf is zero, so current is limited only by small resistance. Current and torque are very large. As speed rises, back emf grows, current falls, and torque falls. That is the cranking curve an engine wants.
T = k φ I<sub>a</sub>      E<sub>b</sub> = k φ ω
blocks.where: T is torque in N·m; k is a constant fixed by the winding design; φ is the flux per pole in webers, set by the field current; I<sub>a</sub> is armature current in A; E<sub>b</sub> is back emf in V; ω is angular speed in rad/s.

blocks.text: A permanent-magnet starter uses ferrite magnets instead of a field winding. It has no field copper, fewer connections, less weight, and no field current. The magnets weaken if overheated or left stalled, so duty cycle matters.

A gear-reduction starter spins a small, fast armature through a planetary or spur gear set, usually 3:1 to 5:1, so the pinion turns slowly with multiplied torque. A lighter motor gives the same cranking torque as a bigger direct-drive one.
A coaxial starter puts the reduction gear on the armature axis, in line with the pinion. It is the most compact arrangement and suits tight engine bays.

Design variations follow the engine. Small petrol engines use permanent-magnet gear-reduction starters; large diesels in trucks use bigger series-wound starters, sometimes at 24 V, and some use sliding-gear starters that move the pinion into mesh in two stages, first slowly at low power and then at full power, so the large teeth mesh without damage. Start-stop cars use reinforced starters built for many more starts in their life.
The drive pushes the pinion into mesh with the flywheel ring gear, passes cranking torque, and releases when the engine fires.

A Bendix inertia drive carries the pinion on a coarse helical screw thread on the armature shaft. When the motor spins, the pinion lags because of inertia and screws forward into mesh. When the engine fires and over-runs the starter, it drives the pinion back and it disengages. It is cheap and needs no solenoid for meshing, but teeth can clash if pinion tooth meets ring-gear tooth.

A pre-engaged drive uses the solenoid to swing a lever that pushes the pinion into mesh before the main contacts close. The motor gets current only after the teeth are in mesh, so there is no clash. Most cars use this.

An overrunning clutch (roller clutch) inside the pinion makes the drive one-way. The armature can turn the pinion, but the pinion cannot turn the armature, so a firing engine does not spin the starter to destruction. A pre-engaged drive always has one.
An armature shift drive pulls the whole armature axially with a solenoid so the pinion meshes; the same movement closes the contacts. It appears on older designs.

Two circuits work together. The power circuit runs from battery positive, through a heavy cable, the solenoid contacts and the motor to earth, and carries 150 A to 400 A. The control circuit runs from the ignition switch through the relay coil to the solenoid coils. Its relay coil side carries 0.1 A to 0.3 A. The terminal 50 line that feeds the solenoid coils carries about 40 A while the plunger moves and about 10 A once the main contacts close. Both are small compared with the power circuit, but they are not the same current.

DIN terminal numbers name the nodes. Terminal 30 is battery positive, unswitched. Terminal 15 is ignition-switched positive. Terminal 50 is the starter control line. The solenoid has two coils: a pull-in coil (heavy wire, about 30 A) that also feeds the motor terminal so the armature turns slowly during meshing, and a hold-in coil (about 10 A) that keeps the plunger home after the contacts close.

items: Key turns to START: the ignition switch feeds the starter relay coil.
The relay coil draws 0.1 A to 0.3 A and closes its contact, feeding terminal 50 of the solenoid.
Pull-in and hold-in coils energise together, about 40 A in total; the plunger pulls the lever and the pinion moves into mesh.
Plunger travel closes the main contacts from terminal 30 to the motor terminal. The contacts short out the pull-in coil, so only the hold-in coil (about 10 A) keeps the plunger in.
The motor cranks, the engine fires, the key is released, the solenoid drops out, and a spring returns the pinion.

blocks.text: A neutral or clutch safety switch sits in series in the terminal 50 line, so the motor cannot crank while a gear is selected. An immobiliser adds one more series contact in the same line.

figure.caption: The two circuits of a pre-engaged starter. The key works a relay coil (0.2 A); its contact feeds terminal 50 and the solenoid coils (40 A, then 10 A once the pull-in coil is shorted out); the plunger closes the main contacts, and 250 A flows from terminal 30 through the motor.

examples.question: A starter draws 250 A at 10.5 V for 2.0 s during a crank. Find (a) the charge taken from the battery in coulombs and in ampere-hours, (b) the electrical power at the starter terminals, and (c) the energy delivered to the starter.
steps: Power delivered to the starter at its terminals: P = V I = 10.5 V × 250 A = 2625 W.
Energy delivered to the starter: E = P t = 2625 W × 2.0 s = 5250 J. The battery supplies slightly more because of internal resistance and cable drop.
examples.answer: The crank takes 500 C (0.139 Ah) from the battery. The starter receives 2625 W and 5250 J at its terminals; the battery supplies slightly more because of internal and cable losses.

V = 10.5
I = 250.0
t = 2.0
Q = I * t
Ah = Q / 3600
P = V * I
E = P * t
print(round(Q, 3))
print(round(Ah, 3))
print(round(P, 3))
print(round(E, 3))

examples.question: A gear-reduction starter has its armature running at 8000 rpm with a torque of 0.80 N·m while cranking. The planetary gear is 4.5:1, the pinion has 10 teeth and the flywheel ring gear 130 teeth, and the gears together are 90 % efficient. The motor draws 110 A at 10.5 V. Find (a) the overall gear ratio, (b) the cranking speed and the torque at the crankshaft, (c) the armature output power and the power at the crankshaft, and (d) the motor efficiency.
steps: Crankshaft torque = armature torque × ratio × efficiency = 0.80 × 58.5 × 0.90 = 42.1 N·m.
Armature output power: ω = 2π × 8000 ÷ 60 = 837.8 rad/s; P = 0.80 × 837.8 = 670 W.
Crankshaft power: ω = 2π × 136.8 ÷ 60 = 14.32 rad/s; P = 42.1 × 14.32 = 603 W, which is 670 W × 0.90, as it must be.
Electrical input = 10.5 V × 110 A = 1155 W. Motor efficiency = 670 ÷ 1155 × 100 = 58 %.
examples.answer: The overall ratio is 58.5, so the engine is cranked at 136.8 rpm with 42.1 N·m; the armature gives 670 W and the crankshaft receives 603 W; the motor is 58 % efficient. A small, fast armature thus gives a large cranking torque through the gears.

traps: The ignition switch does not carry starter current. It works a relay or solenoid; a switch that carried 250 A would weld its contacts in weeks.
Pull-in and hold-in coils are not both active all the time. Once the main contacts close they short the pull-in coil; only the hold-in coil keeps the plunger in.
Terminal 30 is battery positive (unswitched) and terminal 50 is the control line. Swapping them sends cranking current through the key switch.
The pinion must disengage after the engine fires. Without a working overrunning clutch or return spring, the engine spins the starter and destroys it.

quiz.q: Name the DIN terminal numbers for battery positive, ignition-switched positive, and the starter control line.
quiz.a: Terminal 30 is battery positive, terminal 15 is ignition-switched positive, and terminal 50 is the starter control line.

quiz.q: Why does a series-wound motor give its highest torque at zero speed?
quiz.a: At standstill there is no back emf, so armature current is limited only by small resistance. The same large current flows in the series field, so flux is high. Torque T = k φ I<sub>a</sub> is maximum at zero speed and falls as back emf builds.

quiz.q: A starter draws 180 A at 11 V for 1.5 s. Find the charge in coulombs and in Ah, the power, and the energy.
What does the overrunning clutch do, and why is it needed?
quiz.a: It is a one-way roller clutch inside the pinion. The armature can drive the pinion, but the pinion cannot drive the armature. When the engine fires and runs faster than the starter, the clutch slips so the starter is not spun at engine speed.

quiz.q: Compare a Bendix inertia drive with a pre-engaged drive on meshing, clash of teeth, and control.
quiz.a: The Bendix drive meshes by inertia on a helical thread once the motor spins, so power is applied before mesh and teeth can clash. The pre-engaged drive moves the pinion into mesh with the solenoid lever first and closes the main contacts afterwards, so there is no clash. It needs a solenoid and a terminal 50 control line; the Bendix drive does not.

quiz.q: Name four types of starter motor classified by their motor and gearing (not by their drive).

beyond: Not for the exam. Start-stop systems restart the engine in a fraction of a second at a traffic signal, using a reinforced starter, a crank position sensor and a battery monitor; belt-driven and integrated starter-generators combine cranking and charging on mild hybrids. Search for integrated starter-generator and DIN 72552.
